title: What’s New
text:
Theorist + theorist-critic pair
A first-class pair for formal theory sections — assumptions, definitions, lemmas, theorems, and proofs calibrated to top methods journals (Econometrica, Journal of Econometrics, Quantitative Economics, Annals of Statistics).
The theorist drafts identification results, consistency, asymptotic normality, influence functions, DML, bootstrap validity, test properties, and comparative-static propositions. Paper-type aware — activates for econometric methods, theory+empirics, structural identification, and methodological reduced-form papers.
The theorist-critic reviews through 4 sequential phases with early-stop on critical gaps: triage, proof validity (logical, measurability, expansions, identification, asymptotic distribution), assumption minimality + statement calibration, citations + linkage + polish.
Field-specific anchors live in a new Theoretical Foundational References table in domain-profile.md; broad defaults cover DiD, IV, RDD, DML, semiparametric efficiency, GMM, and bootstrap. A Paper Author Team table lets the critic avoid lecturing authors on results they themselves wrote.
Scoring: 20% weight in the aggregate when a theory section is present, renormalized otherwise. Invoke via /strategize theory [target] or audit via /review --theory [target].

Self-citation check surfaces author self-citations missing from Bibliography_base.bib.

title: Architecture
text:
Three-level progressive loading
The system loads context in three stages, each gated by need:









Level
Trigger
Contents
Budget




1 — Metadata
Always (skill index)
Name, description, argument-hint
~100 tokens


2 — SKILL.md body
User invokes the skill
Workflow steps, dispatch logic, modes
< 5k tokens


3 — Bundled files
Agent reads on demand
Templates, gotchas, checklists, references
Unlimited



Level 1 costs almost nothing — every skill’s frontmatter is visible in the skill index, so the system knows what commands exist without loading their bodies. Level 2 activates only when the user types the slash command. Level 3 loads only the specific files the agent needs for the task at hand.

title: Architecture
text:
Skill folder structure
Skills share one layout:
skill-name/
├── SKILL.md          # Routing + dispatch logic (Level 2)
├── gotchas.md        # Known failure points, edge cases
├── templates/        # Reusable artifacts the agent loads
├── references/       # Domain-specific reference material
└── config/           # Machine-readable configuration
Not every skill uses every subfolder. The /write skill has templates/ (paragraph moves, section templates, cleanup patterns) and references/ (notation protocol). The /review skill has templates/ (review checklists, referee report template, disposition pool) and config/ (scoring rubrics). The /strategize skill has templates/ (strategy memo structure, PAP templates, theory memo) and references/ (PAP interview flow). Each skill carries exactly the knowledge its agents need.

title: Architecture
text:
The wiring
When a skill dispatches an agent, it tells the agent which templates to read. The agent file says “read the templates provided by the invoking skill.” This separation means:

Skills own the WHAT — what to produce, what structure to follow, what pitfalls to avoid.
Agents own the HOW — voice, reasoning approach, quality standards.

The same agent can serve multiple skills. The coder-critic reviews output from both /analyze and /review --code, loading different checklists each time. The strategist produces both strategy memos and pre-analysis plans, guided by different templates from the same skill folder.

title: Architecture
text:
Gotchas as first-class content
Thirteen of the 18 skills have a gotchas.md — the highest-signal file in the folder. (/coherence, /dashboard, /deepread, /explain, and /paper-format have none.) These are known failure modes, accumulated from real pipeline runs. The strategist’s gotchas warn that “staggered adoption does not automatically mean DiD is the right choice.” The writer’s gotchas note that “the cleanup pass can over-correct domain-specific hedging that’s actually appropriate.” The review skill’s gotchas document when cold-read critics produce false positives.
Gotchas are the fastest path to quality improvement. When a failure recurs, it gets a line in gotchas.md. The agent reads it before execution. The failure stops recurring.

title: Architecture
text:
What this means in practice
Adding a new template no longer requires editing a 400-line agent prompt. We create a file in templates/, reference it from SKILL.md, and the agent picks it up on next invocation. Knowledge accumulates in skill folders without bloating agent context. Agents stay lean enough to load fast and focused enough to execute well.

title: Architecture
text:
Reading an entry
Each entry declares seven fields: PHASE, PARALLEL_GROUP, REQUIRES, PRODUCES, CRITIC, ESCALATION_TARGET, and QUALITY_WEIGHT.
Here is the strategist entry, annotated:
## strategist
- PHASE: Strategy
- PARALLEL_GROUP: strategy
- REQUIRES: quality_reports/literature/{project}/
             OR quality_reports/data-assessment/{project}/
- PRODUCES: quality_reports/strategy/{project}/
    - Required files: strategy_memo.md
    - Required sections: Estimand, Specification, Assumptions,
                         Robustness Plan, Threats
- CRITIC: strategist-critic
- ESCALATION_TARGET: User --- fundamental design question
- QUALITY_WEIGHT: 25% (identification validity)
The REQUIRES field uses OR logic — the strategist can activate after literature review alone, data assessment alone, or both. The PRODUCES field specifies not just the output file but the sections that must appear in it. pipeline.py check-post (see Lifecycle Validation) checks that these sections exist before the pipeline advances.

title: Architecture
text:
Adding an agent
Create the agent file in .claude/agents/ and add its entry to permissions.md. Two more edits when they apply: add the agent to the orchestrator’s Agent(...) roster if the orchestrator dispatches it, and to quality-gates.json if it carries a weight. scripts/check_scaffold.py fails on a roster name with no agent file and on a weight that differs between the two files. Step-by-step in the Customization Guide.

title: Architecture
text:
PRE-dispatch checks
python3 scripts/pipeline.py check-pre <agent> verifies the agent’s REQUIRES: paths exist and directories are non-empty, critic scores and verdicts in the research journal meet their thresholds, and OR / AND clauses combine as written. Exit 1 means the agent is not dispatched.

title: Architecture
text:
POST-completion checks
python3 scripts/pipeline.py check-post <agent> verifies that the PRODUCES artifacts exist and contain their required sections. Exit 1 means the pipeline does not advance; the Orchestrator re-dispatches the agent with the gaps noted. A critic’s result gates the next agent, so it is checked by that agent’s check-pre.
Each condition prints PASS, FAIL, or MANUAL. MANUAL marks a condition only judgment can settle (for example, “Research idea or research spec”); the Orchestrator decides it and says how.

title: Architecture
text:
What failure looks like
check-pre coder
  FAIL   `quality_reports/strategy/minwage/strategy_memo.md` missing or empty
  FAIL   strategist-critic has no verdict in the research journal
Cannot dispatch coder: `quality_reports/strategy/minwage/strategy_memo.md` missing or empty
No agent launches with missing inputs. No agent advances with missing outputs. The Orchestrator reports the failure to the user along with the skill that produces the missing input (here, /strategize).

title: Architecture
text:
Cold-read enforcement
On every round, the critic receives only: the artifact, its scoring rubric, the severity level, and the content invariants from Rules & Invariants. It does not receive what round this is, what the worker struggled with, prior critic reports, or the research journal. This prevents the critic from softening its evaluation because it knows the worker has already tried twice.
Round-aware feedback (what to fix and how) flows from the Orchestrator to the worker, never through the critics.

title: Architecture
text:
Separation of powers
Critics never create artifacts. Creators never self-score. Every critic’s and referee’s tool list is read-only (Read, Grep, Glob), so a critic cannot write to scripts/ or paper/ in the first place. If a creator reports its own score, the Orchestrator discards it and dispatches the critic.
A critic who fixes its own findings has incentive to find only fixable issues. Separation keeps criticism honest.

title: Architecture
text:
Synthesis rules
A critic passes the artifact with a score of 80 or more; the strategist-critic passes it with a verdict of SOUND or MINOR ISSUES.

Both pass: Artifact advances.
One fails: Worker fixes issues from the failing critic. Both critics re-evaluate.
Both fail: Escalate per the pair’s ESCALATION_TARGET.

title: Architecture
text:
Independence
Neither critic sees the other’s report. The Orchestrator synthesizes both scores independently. This is the same cold-read principle applied across critics, not just across rounds.

title: Architecture
text:
Scope
Dual-critic dispatch activates only for gate artifacts in the full pipeline (/new-project). Standalone skill invocations (/review, /write, etc.) use single critics.

title: Architecture
text:
The state file
Nobody maintains quality_reports/pipeline_state.json by hand. python3 scripts/pipeline.py status derives it from the research journal and the registry: which agents have run, with rounds and latest result; which can be dispatched now; which are waiting and on what; the overall score; and the first gate that fails. title: Architecture
text:
Session recovery
After compaction or a resume, the post-compact-restore.py SessionStart hook prints the active plan, the pipeline state, and the last SESSION_REPORT.md entry into the new context (see Hooks & Automation). Claude reads the files it names and checks git status before continuing. In a fresh session, start from pipeline_state.json and the most recent plan in quality_reports/plans/.

title: Architecture
text:
Execution traces
After a multi-agent skill (/new-project, /analyze, /write full), python3 scripts/pipeline.py traces tabulates rounds, first-pass and final score per agent, and flags HIGH-PERF, FRICTION, and USER ESCALATION. The Orchestrator saves that table with a short reading of the patterns to quality_reports/traces/YYYY-MM-DD_trace.md.

title: Architecture
text:
Relationship to the research journal
The research journal is the record: append-only, one entry per agent invocation, and the input to both score.py and pipeline.py. A critic result that isn’t logged there doesn’t count. pipeline_state.json is a view of the journal, regenerated whenever it is needed.

title: Architecture
text:
Weighted aggregation

title: Quick Start
text:
Research papers have a production function: identify, estimate, write, submit. This scaffold automates each stage with specialized agents that create, review, and gate-check every artifact before it advances. One Claude Code configuration handles the full pipeline — from literature review to journal submission.
Works for empirical economics out of the box. Adapts to labor, public, health, development, trade, IO, and other applied fields by customizing the domain profile and journal profiles.

title: Quick Start
text:
What to Expect
When you run a command, Claude dispatches specialized agents, scores output against quality gates, and presents the results. Before a multi-agent pipeline run or a change across many files, it writes a plan and waits for your approval; smaller tasks go ahead without one. This is not autocomplete — it is an orchestrated pipeline where every artifact is created by one agent and reviewed by another before advancing.
The pipeline at a glance:

Discovery — literature search and data assessment, producing an annotated bibliography and ranked dataset list.
Strategy — identification design, producing a strategy memo with assumptions, pseudo-code, and robustness plan.
Execution — analysis code and paper manuscript, producing scripts, tables, figures, and LaTeX sections.
Review — simulated peer review, producing scored referee reports and an editorial decision.
Submission — replication packaging and quality gate enforcement (aggregate score >= 95, all components >= 80, and the understanding gate: a passing /explain quiz for every script behind a paper exhibit).

You can enter at any stage. Each phase produces structured output saved to quality_reports/.

title: Rules & Invariants
text:
The system enforces quality through rule files — machine-readable documents that tell each agent what to check, what to flag, and how severely to penalize violations. Every critic reads the relevant rules before reviewing. Every worker reads them before creating.
This page is a reference for all 13 rule files, the 26 content invariants, the severity gradient, and the quality gates. If you fork the repo and change nothing else, these rules still apply.

title: Rules & Invariants
text:
How rules load
Six rules load in every session: content-invariants, logging, meta-governance, quality, understanding, and workflow. The other seven (agents, content-standards, lifecycle, paper-organization, permissions, revision, working-paper-format) carry paths: frontmatter and load when Claude reads a matching file — the paper rules on paper/** or a .tex file, the pipeline rules on .claude/agents/** or quality_reports/**.
The reason is cost: every always-loaded line is paid for in every session, whether or not the task needs it. Together with CLAUDE.md, the always-loaded rules come to 679 lines, down from 1,817, and scripts/check_scaffold.py fails if they exceed a 700-line budget. Because a scoped rule loads only on a matching read, the agents and skills that depend on one name it explicitly: the writer-critic and verifier read paper-organization.md and working-paper-format.md, the orchestrator reads permissions.md and lifecycle.md, and /revise reads revision.md.

title: Rules & Invariants
text:
What each file governs
agents.md defines the adversarial pairing system. Every worker has a paired critic. Critics never create artifacts; creators never self-score. When a pair fails to converge after 3 rounds, the file specifies where to escalate (often back to the user for fundamental disagreements).
content-invariants.md lists the 26 non-negotiable rules that every agent checks. These are the “constitution” of the system — violations produce deductions, not suggestions (INV-26 is the exception: a pass/fail gate, never a score). Critics cite invariant numbers (e.g., “violates INV-3”) in their reports. See Content Invariants for the full table.
content-standards.md specifies how the tabular body, figures, and PDFs should look. It covers booktabs formatting, coefficient display conventions (including AEA no-stars policy), preferred R packages (modelsummary, fixest::etable), figure typography (serif fonts, no in-plot titles), reading PDFs with page ranges, and the exploration folder lifecycle. Table 1, the table and figure wrappers, and float placement live in paper-organization.md.
lifecycle.md defines PRE-dispatch and POST-completion validation. scripts/pipeline.py check-pre <agent> checks that required inputs exist and that the critic results they depend on are in the research journal; check-post <agent> checks that the declared outputs exist with their required sections. Each condition prints PASS, FAIL, or MANUAL. This prevents launching agents with missing inputs or advancing past agents with missing outputs.
logging.md standardizes three persistence mechanisms: the session report (append-only human-readable log), the research journal (structured agent-by-agent entries with scores and verdicts), and the pipeline state JSON. The research journal is the record: scripts/score.py computes scores and scripts/pipeline.py status derives the pipeline state from it, so a critic result that isn’t logged there doesn’t count.
meta-governance.md addresses the repo’s dual nature as both a working project and a public template. The “one rule” is simple: before committing, ask whether another researcher forking the repo would benefit. Project-specific state goes in .claude/state/; reusable patterns go in the repo itself. It also governs learning promotion — patterns validated across 3+ projects can be elevated to new invariants, but only with user approval.
paper-organization.md is the house style and the single source for float placement, Table 1, the table and figure wrappers, and section order (INV-23, INV-24, INV-25). Section files hold prose and \cref{} only; tables and figures sit in TABLES and FIGURES blocks at the end of main.tex. /paper-format applies it; the writer-critic deducts for deviations and the verifier fails on them.
permissions.md is the agent registry. Each agent’s entry declares its phase, parallel group, required inputs, expected outputs, paired critic, escalation target, and quality weight. The Orchestrator reads this file to determine what to dispatch and when, and scripts/pipeline.py parses it for the dispatch checks. Adding a new agent means adding an entry here, plus the orchestrator’s Agent(...) roster if the orchestrator dispatches it and quality-gates.json if it carries a weight; scripts/check_scaffold.py fails if the weights in the two files disagree.
quality.md defines how individual critic scores aggregate into the project-wide score that gates submission. scripts/score.py does the arithmetic, from the research journal and .claude/skills/new-project/config/quality-gates.json. It also specifies the severity gradient — the same violation costs more in later phases. See Severity Gradient and Quality Gates for details.
revision.md handles the R&R cycle. When real referee reports arrive, /revise classifies each comment as NEW ANALYSIS (routed to coder), CLARIFICATION (routed to writer), DISAGREE (flagged for user), or MINOR (writer handles directly). The system never autonomously pushes back on referees — DISAGREE items always require human judgment.
understanding.md covers the comprehension gate (INV-26). Every script that produces a paper exhibit needs a current explainer and a passing quiz attempt; /explain writes both. The gate is pass/fail at /submit and a warning at /write results, and it never enters the weighted score: a quiz result is a fact about the author, not the artifact.
workflow.md covers when to write a plan and get approval (before multi-agent pipeline runs and changes across many files; smaller tasks proceed without one), the orchestrator’s dependency-driven loop (identify, dispatch, review, verify, score), standalone vs. pipeline mode, and context management (/checkpoint before /compact, session recovery). The fuller advice on when to compact, rewind, or clear is in the User Guide.
working-paper-format.md specifies the document class and layout, the design choices in the reference preamble (paper/preambles/header.tex), title page conventions, abstract metadata, and bibliography setup; section order follows paper-organization.md. It distinguishes required items (blocking deductions if violated) from recommended items (advisory, no penalty). The writer-critic checks every paper against this standard.

title: Rules & Invariants
text:
Invariants by Category

Paper (INV-1 through INV-13)
Most paper invariants enforce standard economics formatting that journals expect. A few deserve explanation:
INV-4 (significance stars) adapts to the target journal. AEA journals prohibit significance stars entirely — report standard errors and confidence intervals instead. Working papers default to the * p < 0.10, ** p < 0.05, *** p < 0.01 convention. The journal profile determines which convention applies.
INV-7 (notation consistency) catches a common drafting problem: using \(\beta\) for the treatment effect in Section 3 but \(\delta\) in Section 6, or using \(i\) for individuals in one place and firms in another. The same symbol must mean the same thing everywhere.
INV-8 (causal claims need identification) prevents the most common referee complaint in empirical economics. If you write “X causes Y,” you need an identification section explaining how you separate causation from correlation. Descriptive papers should not use causal language at all.
INV-11 (numbers match) catches stale values — when you re-run the analysis and get 0.045 but the text still says 0.052 from a previous run. The writer-critic cross-references every number in the text against the tables and figures.
INV-13 (bare tabular export) enforces the division of labor between code and paper. R/Python/Julia scripts produce the raw table content. The main.tex file wraps it with \begin{table}, \caption{}, and notes. This means you can change a caption without re-running code, and code changes automatically flow into the paper.


Code (INV-14 through INV-19)
Code invariants enforce reproducibility and portability:
INV-14 (single seed) ensures stochastic results are reproducible. One set.seed() call at the top of the master script, not scattered throughout. Multiple seeds make debugging non-deterministic failures nearly impossible.
INV-16 (no absolute paths) is the single most common portability failure. Code that works on your machine but breaks on a collaborator’s because of /Users/yourname/... paths is not reproducible code. Use here::here() in R, pathlib.Path in Python, or joinpath(@__DIR__, ...) in Julia.
INV-19 (prohibited functions) bans functions that break reproducibility or are dangerous in production. setwd() changes global state and breaks when paths differ across machines. rm(list = ls()) destroys the workspace and breaks interactive debugging. install.packages() in scripts is a side effect that should not run automatically.


Talk (INV-20 through INV-21)
Talk invariants enforce fidelity between the presentation and the paper:
INV-20 (notation matches) prevents the common problem of simplifying notation for slides and introducing inconsistencies. If the paper uses \(\hat{\beta}_{ATT}\), the slides must use the same symbol — not \(\beta\) or \(\hat{\tau}\).
INV-21 (traceable claims) prevents “orphan results” that appear on slides but not in the paper. Every number, every claim, every figure on a slide must trace back to the manuscript.


Traceability (INV-22)
INV-22 (claim-source map) is the audit trail. Every numerical claim in the manuscript — “treatment effect of 4.5 percentage points” — must have an entry in quality_reports/claim_source_map_{project}.md that traces it to a specific script line and output file. This makes it possible for a referee (or a future you) to verify any number in the paper by following the chain from text to table to code.


Paper house style (INV-23 through INV-25)
These encode the house layout in paper-organization.md, which coauthors and target journals expect. /paper-format applies them; the writer-critic deducts and the verifier fails on violations.
INV-23 (floats at end) keeps section files to prose and \cref{}. Every table and figure lives in the TABLES and FIGURES blocks after the bibliography in main.tex.
INV-24 (Table 1) fixes the first table as a two-group comparison at baseline. The N lives in unit-count rows at the bottom, not in a column, and there is deliberately no difference or test column.
INV-25 (wrappers) gives every table the same threeparttable wrapper with exhaustive notes (sample, variable definitions, specification columns, SE clustering, stars) and every figure the same subcaption wrapper.
INV-5 (abstract length) and INV-24 are also checked mechanically by scripts/paper_coherence.py, the deterministic layer of /coherence, which flags an abstract over 150 words and a Table 1 with extra columns.


Understanding (INV-26)
INV-26 (comprehension gate) asks whether you can explain the code, not whether it is correct. Every script that writes to paper/tables/ or paper/figures/ needs a current explainer in quality_reports/explainers/ and a passing quiz attempt; when the script changes, its fingerprint changes and the gate reopens. /explain produces both. It is pass/fail at /submit (python3 scripts/explainer_status.py --gate) and never enters the score. See .claude/rules/understanding.md.

The Per-Component Minimum
For submission, the aggregate score must be >= 95 and no individual component can be below 80 and every non-conditional component must be scored. A perfect literature review cannot compensate for broken identification. A beautiful manuscript cannot compensate for code that does not reproduce. A missing referee report cannot be renormalized away.
This rule prevents the “average-up” problem — where excellence in one area masks serious deficiencies in another.

title: Rules & Invariants
text:
Recovering from a Low Score
When a score falls below the gate threshold:

The Orchestrator identifies which components are blocking
It re-dispatches the relevant worker-critic pair to fix the flagged issues
After fixes, the critic re-reviews (up to 3 rounds per pair)
If 3 rounds fail, the system escalates — often back to the user for a design decision

The goal is convergence, not perfection on the first pass. Most artifacts reach 80+ by round 2.






WarningThe submission gate is intentionally high



A score of 95 is difficult to achieve. It requires all components to be polished, all robustness checks to pass, and the simulated referees to find no fatal issues. This is by design — the system should flag problems before a journal does, not after. If the gate feels too strict, the alternative is a rejected paper.

title: Agents
text:
The system uses 25 specialized agents, most of them organized into worker-critic pairs. Four rules explain most of the system’s behavior.


Every creator has a paired destroyer. The critic reads the artifact, scores it against a rubric, and lists what must change — but never edits the file itself. The strategist-critic gives a verdict instead of points: SOUND, MINOR ISSUES, MAJOR ISSUES, or CRITICAL ERRORS. If the score falls below 80 (or the verdict is MAJOR ISSUES or worse), the worker revises and the critic re-evaluates. This cycle repeats up to 3 rounds.

The coherence pair is a chain rather than a loop: /coherence --deep runs coherence-finder once per check group, one coherence-skeptic per group tries to refute its findings, and coherence-consolidator merges the survivors. No scores, no revision rounds (see Coherence Chain).
Nine agents have no paired critic. Two are infrastructure (orchestrator, verifier); three already serve as reviewers (editor, domain-referee, methods-referee); two are later stages of the coherence chain (coherence-skeptic, coherence-consolidator). The explainer’s output is tested on the author by a quiz, not scored by a critic. The guide-writer writes documentation, outside the research pipeline.



Critics never create. Creators never self-score. Every critic’s tool list is read-only (Read, Grep, Glob), so a critic cannot write a file in scripts/, paper/, or anywhere else. If a creator reports its own score, the orchestrator discards it and dispatches the critic.
This prevents the system from rubber-stamping its own output. A critic who fixes their own findings has incentive to find only fixable issues. Separation keeps criticism honest.



Critics evaluate blind. On every round, the critic receives only the artifact, its scoring rubric, the severity level, and the content invariants. It does not receive: what round this is, what the worker struggled with, prior critic reports, or the research journal. A critic that knows the worker has already tried twice will soften its evaluation. The cold-read protocol prevents this drift.



Three strikes, then escalation. If a worker-critic pair cannot converge after 3 rounds, the orchestrator routes the problem elsewhere — either to a different agent or to the user. Escalation targets are declared per agent in permissions.md. When the coder and coder-critic deadlock, the issue escalates to the strategist-critic (is the memo implementable?). When the strategist and strategist-critic deadlock, it escalates to the user (fundamental design question). This prevents infinite loops while ensuring hard problems get human judgment.

title: Agents
text:
Discovery Pair
The librarian searches top-5 general-interest journals, field journals, NBER working papers, and citation chains to produce an annotated bibliography, a BibTeX file, a frontier map (what has been done), and a positioning statement (where the new paper fits). The explorer searches for datasets — public, administrative, survey — and grades each by feasibility: variable coverage, access requirements, panel structure, and known data issues.
Both run in parallel from the start of a project. Neither depends on the other. The librarian-critic checks for coverage gaps (missing seminal papers, missing methods literature, over-reliance on working papers). The explorer-critic checks measurement validity (does the proposed variable actually capture the concept?) and identification compatibility (does this data support the likely design?).
Together they answer a single question: what has been done, and what data could let us do something new?
Activates: From a research idea or spec. No prerequisites. Produces: quality_reports/literature/ and quality_reports/data-assessment/ Quality gate: No score gate. Strategy needs only one of the two outputs to exist (literature OR data assessment); both critics’ scores feed the weighted aggregate, 10% each.

title: Agents
text:
Strategy Pair
The strategist is paper-type aware. Given the literature and data assessment, it classifies the paper type (reduced-form, structural, theory+empirics, descriptive) and applies the corresponding strategy template. For reduced-form papers, it assesses the identification landscape, proposes designs ranked by credibility, and specifies design-specific estimation guidance (modern DiD estimators for staggered treatment, effective F for IV, MSE-optimal bandwidth for RDD). For structural papers, it specifies the model environment, decision problem, equilibrium concept, identification of each parameter, and counterfactual design. It always anticipates the top 5 referee objections.
The theorist activates conditionally — only for papers that need formal proofs. It drafts assumptions, definitions, propositions, and proofs at journal-publication rigor, with every theorem linked to the empirical strategy. Its critic runs a 4-phase proof review with early stopping on logical gaps.
The strategist-critic is the system’s most important gatekeeper. It runs a 4-phase sequential audit: identify the design, check whether the core assumptions hold (design-specific checklists), evaluate inference and code-theory alignment, then check robustness. Critical finding in Phase 2 stops the review — no point checking robustness if parallel trends are violated.
Activates: After at least one Discovery output (literature OR data assessment). Produces: quality_reports/strategy/ and (when activated) quality_reports/theory/ Quality gate: Strategist-critic verdict of SOUND or MINOR ISSUES before Execution activates; theorist-critic >= 80 when the theorist ran.

title: Agents
text:
Execution Trio
The data-engineer takes raw data and produces clean, analysis-ready datasets. It documents every sample restriction with counts, constructs variables per strategy memo definitions, merges datasets with documented merge rates, and produces publication-quality figures (custom themes, colorblind-safe palettes, no titles inside plots).
The coder translates the strategy memo into numbered analysis scripts (00_master.R through 07_tables.R) with engineering discipline: numerical guards, pre-allocation, a single seed, here() for all paths, and a paper-to-code naming map linking every \(\beta\) and \(Y_{it}\) to its code variable. It implements the main specification, all robustness checks from the memo, and exports bare tabular environments for tables.
The writer drafts the manuscript after code is approved. It refuses to write Results without actual output files in paper/tables/ — this gate exists because the distinction between “the strategy predicts X” and “the data shows X” is the difference between a proposal and a paper. It maintains a claim-source map tracing every numerical claim to a specific script line and output file.
The coder-critic reviews both the data-engineer and coder across 16 categories: strategic alignment (does the code match the memo?), code quality (reproducibility, numerics, function design), and infrastructure (checkpointing, error handling, prohibited patterns). The writer-critic runs 8 checks: structure, claims-evidence, identification fidelity, AI-pattern detection, LaTeX format, compilation, voice fidelity, and notation consistency.
Alongside the trio, the explainer runs once code review passes, in parallel with the writer. For each analysis script it writes a delta-explainer (only what departs from the strategy memo, plus a sample-construction ledger with drop counts), a 5-question quiz, and a separate answer key. It tests the author, not the code: /submit blocks until every script behind a paper exhibit has a passing quiz at the script’s current fingerprint (INV-26).
Activates: Data-engineer and coder after a strategist-critic verdict of SOUND or MINOR ISSUES. Writer and explainer after coder-critic score >= 80. Produces: data/cleaned/, scripts/R/, paper/tables/, paper/figures/, paper/sections/ Quality gate: Coder-critic and writer-critic both >= 80 before Peer Review.

title: Agents
text:
Review Team
The editor performs desk review: reads the abstract and introduction, skims the contribution, verifies novelty, and decides whether to send to referees or desk reject. When it sends, it assigns each referee a contrasting intellectual disposition — STRUCTURAL (“where’s the mechanism?”), CREDIBILITY (“show me the pre-trends”), MEASUREMENT (“how is this measured?”), POLICY (“does this generalize?”), THEORY (“what does the model predict?”), or SKEPTIC (“what would make this go away?”). Each referee also receives randomized pet peeves drawn from pools of critical and constructive tendencies.
The domain-referee evaluates substance: contribution and novelty (30%), literature positioning (25%), substantive arguments (20%), external validity (15%), and journal fit (10%). The methods-referee evaluates methods with paper-type-specific weights: identification strategy, estimation, inference, robustness, and replication readiness. Neither sees the other’s report. In round 1 neither sees earlier verdicts either: both read a fenced copy of the manuscript outside the repository, away from quality_reports/reviews/. --peer --r2 deliberately reuses round 1.
After both reports arrive, the editor classifies each concern as FATAL (cannot be fixed), ADDRESSABLE (fixable with revision), or TASTE (referee preference), resolves disagreements with explicit reasoning, and issues a decision.
Activates: After writer-critic and coder-critic both >= 80. Invoked via /review --peer. Produces: quality_reports/reviews/ Quality gate: Editorial decision of Accept or Minor Revisions to proceed to Submission.

title: Agents
text:
Presentation Pair
The storyteller creates talks from the paper in four formats (job market 40–50 slides, seminar 25–35, short 10–15, lightning 3–5) and two output types (Beamer PDF, Quarto RevealJS HTML). Paper-type aware: reduced-form talks lead with the policy question and show variation; structural talks build the model step by step with progressive reveal and pay off with the counterfactual; theory+empirics talks present competing explanations and a distinguishing prediction; descriptive talks lead with what is missing in current measures.
The storyteller-critic checks narrative flow (does the hook work?), visual quality (text overflow, font sizes, one idea per slide), content fidelity (numbers match the paper), and compilation. Presentation scores are advisory — they do not block commits or PRs.
Activates: After writer-critic score >= 80. Can run parallel with Peer Review. Produces: paper/talks/ or paper/quarto/ Quality gate: Advisory only.

title: Agents
text:
Coherence Chain
/coherence --deep adds a reasoning pass on top of the deterministic parser, run as a three-stage chain. The coherence-finder is one definition dispatched once per non-empty check group (specification, claims, continuity, notation, theory), each in its own context, so the groups do not anchor on each other. A coherence-skeptic per group with findings tries to refute each one, defaulting to refuted when uncertain. The coherence-consolidator merges the same defect seen from different checks and ranks what survives.
Activates: On /coherence --deep, after paper_coherence.py --slices writes one slice per group. Produces: A ## Reasoning layer section appended to quality_reports/coherence/YYYY-MM-DD_report.md Quality gate: None. Reasoning findings are advisory and never block; coherence carries no weight in the score.

title: Agents
text:
Infrastructure
The orchestrator is the project manager. It reads permissions.md to determine which agents can activate and runs scripts/pipeline.py check-pre / check-post around every dispatch (do REQUIRES artifacts exist? do PRODUCES artifacts exist with required sections?). It launches worker-critic pairs in parallel when independent and tracks strike counts. It does not do the arithmetic: scripts/score.py computes the weighted score, and pipeline.py status derives pipeline_state.json from the research journal. Its tool list names its dispatch roster as Agent(...), so it can only spawn registry agents. It makes no research decisions — when judgment is needed, it escalates to the user with a clear question.
The verifier checks mechanical correctness in two modes. It starts from scripts/verify.py, which runs the mechanical checks (including the INV-26 understanding gate), and keeps the judgment calls for itself. Standard mode (between phases): LaTeX compilation, script execution, file integrity, output freshness. Submission mode (before journal deposit): package inventory, dependency verification, data provenance, end-to-end execution, output cross-reference, and AEA-format README completeness. It scores binary — 0 or 100, contributing 5% weight to the overall project score.
Activates: Orchestrator runs throughout. Verifier runs between phases and at submission. Produces: quality_reports/pipeline_state.json, quality_reports/verification_report.md Quality gate: Verifier must PASS (100) for submission.

Section walkthrough

**Primary:** Labor Economics
**Adjacent subfields:** Public Finance, Education, Development

| Tier | Journals |
|------|----------|
| Top-5 | AER, Econometrica, JPE, QJE, REStud |
| Top field | JHR, JLE, AEJ:Applied |
| Strong field | RESTAT, JPubE, JDE |
Common Data Sources. What the Explorer looks for first, and what the explorer-critic knows the quirks of.
Common Identification Strategies. What the Strategist considers first. Each row names a strategy, a typical application, and the key assumption to defend.
Field Conventions. Norms the Coder and Writer follow — clustering level, functional form for costs, whether to report LPM alongside logit, whether welfare analysis is expected.
Notation Conventions. Symbol-meaning pairs the Writer enforces. Include anti-patterns to prevent — for example, “Don’t use \(y\) without subscripts.”
Seminal References. Papers the Librarian ensures are cited when relevant. Keep this to 5–15 entries — the landmark papers in your area.
Theoretical Foundational References. Anchor references for the Theorist agent when building or reviewing a formal theory section. Only needed for papers with a theory section (econometric methods, structural, theory+empirics). Leave empty to fall back on the generic econometric theory defaults baked into the theorist agent.
| Topic | Anchor references |
|-------|------------------|

Field-Specific Referee Concerns. Common objections the domain-referee and methods-referee should watch for. Examples: “Selection into treatment,” “External validity — Medicaid population is not general population.”
Quality Tolerance Thresholds. Numerical precision standards for cross-language replication and simulation checks.

title: Customization
text:
Anatomy of a profile entry
Each profile is a structured block of plain-language fields. Here is the AER entry:
### American Economic Review (AER)
**Focus:** All fields of economics --- the broadest audience
**Bar:** Must interest economists outside your subfield. Big question,
        clean execution, clear contribution.
**Domain referee adjusts:** Contribution must be broad. Literature
        positioning against the *general* frontier, not just subfield.
**Methods referee adjusts:** Identification must be convincing to
        non-specialists. Clean, transparent design preferred over
        technically complex one.
**Typical concerns:** "Why should economists outside this field care?"
        "Is the contribution big enough for AER?"
**Referee pool:** CREDIBILITY (high), POLICY (medium), STRUCTURAL (medium),
        MEASUREMENT (low), THEORY (low), SKEPTIC (low)
**Table format:** No significance stars. Standard errors in parentheses.
The Referee pool weights determine which dispositions the simulated editor draws when selecting referees. The two referees always get different dispositions. Six dispositions exist: STRUCTURAL, CREDIBILITY, MEASUREMENT, POLICY, THEORY, SKEPTIC. See Agents for how the editor uses these.

text:

Each agent can set its own effort in frontmatter. The shipped settings put judgment-heavy roles at high (strategist, strategist-critic, theorist, theorist-critic, methods-referee, editor) and narrow checkers at low (coherence-finder, coherence-skeptic, librarian-critic, explorer-critic); the rest use the default. To change one, edit its effort: line.

title: Customization
text:
The steps
1. Create the folder. .claude/skills/[name]/ with SKILL.md (required) and gotchas.md (recommended — 13 of the 18 shipped skills have one).
2. Write SKILL.md with frontmatter. The frontmatter is Level 1 metadata — always loaded, always visible in the skill index. Keep it under 100 tokens.
---
name: [skill-name]
description: [One sentence. What does this skill do?]
argument-hint: "[modes and arguments the user can pass]"
allowed-tools: Read,Write,Edit,Bash,Grep,Glob,Agent,Task
user-invocable: true
---
If the skill dispatches agents, list Agent alongside Task (Task is the old name; check_scaffold.py fails on Task without Agent). Two optional keys: disable-model-invocation: true makes the skill run only when you type it, as /new-project and /deepread do, and disallowed-tools: Edit keeps it from editing files, as /review and /deepread do.
The body of SKILL.md is Level 2 — loaded only when the user invokes the command. It contains workflow steps, dispatch logic, mode routing, and a Bundled Resources table that tells agents which templates to read.
3. Create gotchas.md (recommended). Seed it with known failure points — even two or three lines to start. This file accumulates over time as real pipeline runs surface edge cases. It is the fastest-appreciating asset in the folder.
4. Create templates/. Reusable artifacts the agent loads during execution. A strategy skill carries memo templates and checklist structures. A review skill carries scoring rubrics and report templates. A write skill carries paragraph-move patterns and section templates. Each template is a separate file — the agent reads only what it needs.
5. Optionally: references/ and config/. References hold domain material the agent consults (notation protocols, interview flows, design checklists). Config holds machine-readable settings (scoring weights, disposition pools, threshold mappings).
6. Wire it. In SKILL.md’s dispatch section, tell agents which templates to read. The agent’s own file says “read the templates provided by the invoking skill” — it does not hardcode template paths.

title: Customization
text:
The three-level loading rule
This constraint keeps context budgets predictable:

Level 1 (frontmatter): Loaded always, even when the skill is not triggered. Under 100 tokens. Name, description, argument-hint.
Level 2 (SKILL.md body): Loaded when the user invokes the skill. Under 5k tokens. Workflow, routing, dispatch.
Level 3 (bundled files): Loaded on demand by agents during execution. No token limit. Templates, gotchas, references, config.

The budget discipline matters. If SKILL.md exceeds 5k tokens, split operational detail into templates. If frontmatter exceeds 100 tokens, the skill index bloats and the system pays the cost on every session — even sessions that never invoke the skill.

title: Customization
text:
Example: a minimal custom skill
A /data-diary skill that logs data decisions as the project evolves:
data-diary/
├── SKILL.md
├── gotchas.md
└── templates/
    └── diary-entry.md
The SKILL.md frontmatter:
---
name: data-diary
description: Log data decisions --- variable constructions, sample restrictions, merge choices --- with rationale and alternatives considered.
argument-hint: "[decision summary]"
allowed-tools: Read,Write,Edit
user-invocable: true
---
The body dispatches no agent — it appends a structured entry to quality_reports/data_diary.md using the template in templates/diary-entry.md. The gotchas file warns: “Don’t log trivial renames. Log decisions where a different choice would change results.”

title: Customization
section: When NOT to create a skill
text:
When NOT to create a skill
Not every workflow needs a folder. A one-off task with no templates, no gotchas, no reusable structure is just a task — handle it with an existing skill or directly. The threshold: if we would benefit from the same structure on the next project, it deserves a skill folder. If it is project-specific and unlikely to recur, it does not.

title: Customization

Graduation checklist
To move an exploration into production (scripts/R/, paper/tables/, etc.):

Quality score >= 80
All tests pass
Results replicate within tolerance
Code is clear without deep context

title: Customization
text:
Kill switch
Abandon at any point. Move the folder to ARCHIVE/abandoned_[name]/ with a brief note explaining what was attempted and why it stopped. No guilt — exploration is inherently uncertain.

title: Customization
text:
Auto-memory
Claude Code’s built-in memory system saves corrections and preferences automatically. When you correct Claude (“that’s UAB, not Emory”), it stores the correction in .claude/projects/.../memory/MEMORY.md and applies it in future sessions. You can also explicitly ask Claude to remember or forget something.

The session report records operations, decisions, results, and commits. The research journal records agent invocations, scores, and phase transitions — it is the shared context that lets agents understand what other agents have done.

title: Customization
text:
Compaction discipline
Context windows fill up. When they do, Claude auto-compacts by summarizing the conversation. You lose detail. The countermeasure:

Run /checkpoint before natural stopping points. It saves state to memory, SESSION_REPORT.md, and the research journal.
Prefer manual /compact over letting auto-compression surprise you. You control what gets summarized.
Aim for 5–10 turn focused sessions. Long sessions drift.
Start fresh between phases. Do not carry discovery residue into execution.

After compaction or a new session, Claude reads the most recent checkpoint artifacts, CLAUDE.md, the latest plan, and recent git history to reconstruct context.

title: Customization
text:
The /checkpoint skill
Run /checkpoint before ending a session or compacting. It captures:

Auto-memory updates (corrections, project state, references)
Session report entry (operations, decisions, results)
Research journal entry (agent, phase, score, verdict)
Obsidian project note (optional — if .claude/state/obsidian-config.md is configured)

For details on hooks that fire during compaction and session start, see Hooks.

Peer review details: The editor reads the paper and decides DESK REJECT or SEND TO REFEREES. If sent, the editor assigns each referee a disposition (STRUCTURAL, CREDIBILITY, MEASUREMENT, POLICY, THEORY, or SKEPTIC) plus one critical and one constructive pet peeve from the journal’s referee pool. When a journal name is provided, the entire flow calibrates to that journal’s profile.
R&R rounds: Round 2 skips desk review. Same referees check whether each prior concern was resolved, partially resolved, or not addressed. Round 3 (max) allows Accept, Minor, or Reject only.

title: Command Reference
text:
/coherence
Syntax: /coherence [file path] [--deep] [--fix] [--strict] [--json]
Is the paper internally sound? Not whether it is any good — that is /review. Every deterministic finding is checkable: a reference resolves or it does not, a number appears in the cited table or it does not.
What happens:

Layer 1 (always): scripts/paper_coherence.py checks cross-references, citation keys, \input and graphics targets, claim numbers against the cells of the tables they cite, derived arithmetic, orphan floats, duplicate macros, abstract length (INV-5), and Table 1 columns (INV-24). Standard library only; exits 1 on a blocking finding.
Layer 2 (--deep): coherence-finder runs once per non-empty check group (specification, claims, continuity, notation, theory), each in its own context; one coherence-skeptic per group with findings tries to refute them; coherence-consolidator merges and ranks the survivors.
Save the report and refresh the dashboard.

Modes / Flags:







Invocation
Description




/coherence
Layer 1 over the whole paper


/coherence [file]
Layer 1 scoped to one file


--deep
Layer 1 + the reasoning pass (advisory, never blocks)


--fix
Apply only unambiguous mechanical fixes (a mistyped label, a wrong graphic extension). Never edits a claim number


--strict
Promote minor findings to blocking (before submission)


--json
Emit the index only, no markdown



Agents dispatched: None for Layer 1. With --deep: coherence-finder × check group, coherence-skeptic × group with findings, coherence-consolidator once.
Output artifacts: quality_reports/coherence/YYYY-MM-DD_report.md and quality_reports/coherence/index.json.
What to do next: Fix blocking findings first; the report gives the nearest table cell for each number mismatch. A PASS with 0 table cells indexed means the tables could not be parsed, not that the paper is sound. Run this before /deepread and /review --peer.

What happens:

scripts/deepread.py splits the paper into sections (via paper_coherence.py --segments), each carrying the tables, notes, and equations it cites.
Readers comment on each segment in parallel: general always, rigor if it has equations, evidence if it has tables, skeptic with --skeptic.
One verifier per segment tries to refute each comment; a consolidator merges duplicates and ranks; an overall assessment closes the report.

Description

Pattern
What It Catches

title: Hooks & Automation
text:
Claude Code fires hooks on specific events — before a tool runs, after a file is edited, before context gets compacted. Scripts in .claude/hooks/ register for these events and execute automatically when they fire. You never call them directly.
Hooks serve two purposes: guardrails (blocking operations that would damage the project) and automation (running checks or capturing state without manual intervention).











Event
When It Fires
Blocking?
Use Case




PreToolUse
Before Claude calls a tool (Edit, Write, Bash, etc.)
Yes — exit 2 blocks the tool call
Protect files from accidental edits


PostToolUse
After a tool call completes
No — advisory only
Lint code after edits


PreCompact
Before context compaction
No — a systemMessage shows the user a reminder
Capture session state before memory loss


SessionStart
When a new session begins (including after compaction)
No — advisory only
Restore context from prior session






Claude Code reads a hook’s exit code and any JSON it prints on stdout:

Exit 0 — success. JSON on stdout is honored: permissionDecision: "deny" blocks a tool call, additionalContext puts text in front of Claude, and systemMessage shows the user a warning. Plain stdout reaches Claude only on SessionStart (and UserPromptSubmit); for other events it goes to the debug log. Stderr on exit 0 is never shown.
Exit 2 — blocking error. For PreToolUse it blocks the tool call and shows stderr.
Any other non-zero exit, a timeout, or a script that can’t start — a hook failure. By default the action proceeds and the transcript shows the hook’s name with the first line of stderr. A hook that sets "onFailure": "block" (Claude Code 2.1.295+) turns a failure into a block instead.

One trap: when python3 can’t find the script file it exits 2, so a hook whose .py file is missing or renamed already blocks every matching tool call, with or without onFailure.



Every hook here runs through .claude/hooks/_hooklib.py, which gives each run one of three outcomes:








Outcome
When
What you see




acted
The hook did its job (linted a file, blocked an edit, restored context)
Its output


skipped
Nothing to do (a .txt edit, no guard active)
Nothing


error
The hook could not do its job
A one-line notice in the transcript: clo-author hook <name>: <reason>



What an error does to the action depends on the hook:

Advisory hooks (lint, restore, health, pre-compact) keep the default. The action proceeds and you see the notice.
Guards (protect-files.py, session-guard.py) set "onFailure": "block". A guard that cannot answer blocks the action, because a guard that fails open lets through exactly what it exists to stop. In a test, a corrupted /careful state file let writes through silently under the old setting; with "block" the write stopped and the error named the file.

The cost of failing closed: a broken guard also blocks the edit that would fix it. Fix it by hand in your editor — the error message and hook-health.py name the file. scripts/test_hooks.py and scripts/check_scaffold.py both fail if a PreToolUse hook in settings.json lacks "onFailure": "block".
A payload missing a field the hook depends on is an error, not a skip. Two hooks in this template once sat dead for months because they read a field Claude Code never sends, found it empty, and exited cleanly as if there were nothing to do. require() in _hooklib.py turns that case into a visible failure.
Every outcome is appended to .claude/state/hook-log.jsonl (gitignored). At session start, hook-health.py reads that log and speaks up when something is wrong. python3 scripts/test_hooks.py feeds every hook synthetic payloads and checks all three outcomes.



Hooks are registered in .claude/settings.json under the hooks key. Each event type maps to an array of hook groups, where each group has:

matcher — a regex pattern for filtering. For PreToolUse and PostToolUse, it matches tool names (e.g., "Edit|Write"). For SessionStart, it matches session types (e.g., "compact|resume"). Omit the matcher to fire on every event of that type.
hooks — an array of hook definitions, each with type, command, timeout (in seconds), and optionally onFailure ("continue", the default, or "block").

{
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Edit|Write",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "python3 \"$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR\"/.claude/hooks/protect-files.py",
            "timeout": 5,
            "onFailure": "block"
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
The environment variable $CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR resolves to the project root at runtime. Always use it in hook commands so paths stay portable.

title: Hooks & Automation
Hooks & Automation
text:
1. protect-files.py
Event: PreToolUse (matcher: Edit|Write) | Timeout: 5s | Blocking: Yes | On failure: blocks

What it does
Some files should never be touched by an agent. Strategy memos after approval, referee reports from real journals, the hook configuration itself — these are inputs or infrastructure, not outputs. This hook enforces that boundary.
When Claude attempts an Edit or Write operation, the hook extracts the target file path from the tool input, checks the filename against a list of protected patterns, and blocks the operation if there is a match.


Protected patterns (default)
PROTECTED_PATTERNS = [
    "settings.json",
    "strategy-memo-*.md",
    "referee-report-*.md",
    "quality-score-*.json",
]
These defaults protect:

settings.json — the hook configuration itself. Accidental edits here could disable all hooks.
strategy-memo-*.md — approved strategy memos. The strategist-critic reviews these; Claude should not modify them after approval.
referee-report-*.md — real referee reports. These are external inputs that Claude classifies and responds to, never rewrites.
quality-score-*.json — critic scores. Separation of powers: creators cannot edit their own scores.



How it works

Reads the tool input JSON from stdin and requires tool_input.file_path (a missing path is a visible error)
Compares the basename against each protected pattern with shell-style glob matching (fnmatch)
If a pattern matches, prints a permissionDecision: "deny" with the reason, which blocks the edit
If no pattern matches, exits silently and the edit proceeds



Exit behavior
Exits 0 in both cases; the deny decision travels as JSON. The block message reads: "Protected file: <filename>. Edit it by hand, or remove the pattern '<pattern>' from .claude/hooks/protect-files.py."


Customizing
Add or remove entries in PROTECTED_PATTERNS. Matching is on the basename only (not the full path), so "*.bib" would protect all .bib files regardless of directory. For path-specific protection, compare hook.require("tool_input.file_path") against a full path in body().

title: Hooks & Automation
text:
2. session-guard.py
Event: PreToolUse (matcher: Edit|Write|Bash) | Timeout: 5s | Blocking: Yes | On failure: blocks

What it does
Two guards in one hook, both opt-in. When neither guard is active, the hook reads a single JSON file, finds nothing, and exits — zero overhead in the common case.
Freeze locks edits to a set of allowed directories. Invoke /freeze paper/ and every Write or Edit targeting a file outside paper/ gets blocked. The .claude/ directory is always exempt (we cannot freeze ourselves out of configuration changes).
Careful blocks destructive Bash commands. Invoke /careful and patterns like rm -rf, git reset --hard, and git push --force are intercepted before they execute. Non-destructive Bash commands pass through untouched.


Guard state
Both guards read from a single file: .claude/state/session-guards.json. The /freeze and /careful skills write this file; the hook only reads it.
{
  "freeze": {
    "active": true,
    "allowed_paths": ["paper/", "scripts/"],
    "activated_at": "2026-05-09T14:30:00",
    "reason": "User invoked /freeze"
  },
  "careful": {
    "active": true,
    "activated_at": "2026-05-09T14:30:00",
    "reason": "User invoked /careful"
  }
}


Freeze logic
When freeze.active is true and the tool is Edit or Write:

Extract the target file_path from tool input
If the path is inside .claude/, allow (always editable)
Check against each entry in allowed_paths (resolved relative to project root)
If the file matches an allowed path prefix, allow
Otherwise, block with: "FREEZE ACTIVE: Edit blocked. File '<name>' is outside allowed paths: [<paths>]. Run /freeze off to deactivate."



Careful logic
When careful.active is true and the tool is Bash:

Extract the command string from tool input
Test against a list of destructive regex patterns:




Pattern
What It Catches




rm -(r\|f\|rf\|fr)
Recursive/force delete


git reset --hard
Discard all uncommitted changes


git push --force / git push -f
Overwrite remote history


git clean -f
Delete untracked files


git checkout -- .
Discard all working tree changes


git branch -D
Force-delete branch


DROP TABLE / DROP DATABASE
SQL destruction


chmod 777
Overly permissive permissions




If any pattern matches, block with: "CAREFUL MODE: Blocked '<description>'. Run /careful off to deactivate, or rephrase the command."
If no pattern matches, allow



Exit behavior
When it can answer, the hook exits 0, and blocking is communicated through stdout JSON (hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision: "deny" with a permissionDecisionReason) rather than exit codes — the current Claude Code protocol for PreToolUse decisions. When it cannot (for example, session-guards.json is not valid JSON), it exits 1, and "onFailure": "block" makes Claude Code block the call. Delete or fix the state file by hand to recover.


Activating and deactivating







Command
Effect




/freeze paper/
Only allow edits in paper/


/freeze scripts/ data/
Only allow edits in scripts/ and data/


/freeze off
Deactivate freeze


/careful
Block destructive commands


/careful off
Deactivate careful mode



Both guards stay on until you turn them off — across conversations too, since .claude/state/session-guards.json persists and nothing clears it automatically. If edits are blocked and you don’t remember freezing, check that file or run /freeze off.

title: Hooks & Automation
text:
3. post-edit-lint.py
Event: PostToolUse (matcher: Edit|Write) | Timeout: 10s | Blocking: No (advisory)

What it does
The coder-critic catches prohibited patterns, but it runs later in the pipeline. This hook gives Claude immediate feedback on violations — setwd(), missing set.seed(), sapply() — so it can fix them in the same editing pass rather than waiting for a review cycle.


How it works

Reads the edited file path from the JSON payload Claude Code sends on stdin (tool_input.file_path)
Filters by extension — only runs on .R, .py, and .jl files
Skips files inside .claude/ (hooks, agents, and other configuration scripts should not be linted as analysis code)
Delegates to lint-scripts.sh for the actual analysis
Returns any findings as hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext, which is how a PostToolUse hook puts text in front of Claude (plain stdout only reaches the transcript)



Exit behavior
Always exits 0. Lint findings appear in Claude’s context as advisory information — they inform the agent but do not block the edit.

Not a hook itself — this is the linter that post-edit-lint.py calls. It can also be run standalone via /tools lint.

lint-scripts.sh              # Lint scripts/ in the current project


What it checks
The linter is a grep-based static analyzer organized by language. Every check maps to a specific rule from the coding standards.

Common checks (all languages)

Exit behavior
Always exits 0, even when issues are found. The linter is advisory — it reports problems but never blocks operations. The coder-critic uses these findings to inform its scoring.

title: Hooks & Automation
text:
5. pre-compact.py
Event: PreCompact | Timeout: 10s | Blocking: No (message only)

What it does
Compaction is the single biggest source of context loss in long sessions. This hook captures the current state before context compaction destroys it — the active plan, recent decisions, and a timestamp — so post-compact-restore.py can bring it back afterward.


What it captures

Active plan — finds the most recent non-completed plan in quality_reports/plans/, extracts its status (draft/approved/in-progress) and the first unchecked task
Recent decisions — the last three bullets under Decisions: in the newest SESSION_REPORT.md entry
Compaction timestamp — records when compaction occurred



Where it saves
State is written to a JSON file at ~/.claude/sessions/<project-hash>/pre-compact-state.json, where <project-hash> is an MD5 hash of the project directory. This location is outside the project tree, so it does not clutter the repository.


Side effects

Prints a context survival checklist to the transcript as a reminder:

Context Survival Checklist:
  [ ] Active plan saved to quality_reports/plans/
  [ ] SESSION_REPORT.md updated
  [ ] Open questions documented


Exit behavior
Always exits 0, so compaction is never blocked. The checklist reaches you as a systemMessage (stderr on exit 0 would go only to the debug log). It is a reminder to run /checkpoint before compaction if you have not already.

title: Hooks & Automation
text:
6. post-compact-restore.py
Event: SessionStart (matcher: compact|resume) | Timeout: 5s | Blocking: No (advisory)

What it does
Restores context after compaction by reading the state saved by pre-compact.py and printing it into the new session. Claude resumes with immediate awareness of the active plan, the current task, and the last three decisions made before compaction.


How it works

Reads the source field of the SessionStart payload and runs only for compact or resume (not on fresh starts)
Reads and deletes the pre-compact-state.json file (one-time consumption)
Finds the active plan, summarizes quality_reports/pipeline_state.json, and reads the newest SESSION_REPORT.md entry’s status
Prints a plain-text restoration message (no terminal color codes, since SessionStart stdout goes straight into Claude’s context) ending with: read the active plan and check git status before continuing



Exit behavior
Exits 0 when it restores (or has nothing to restore). An error exits 1 with a one-line notice; session start proceeds either way, since the hook keeps the default onFailure.


Why the pair exists
Without these hooks, Claude resumes after compaction with no memory of the active plan, current task, or recent decisions. The pre-compact/post-compact pair ensures continuity — the first hook captures state, the second restores it.

title: Hooks & Automation
text:
7. hook-health.py
Event: SessionStart (matcher: startup|resume) | Timeout: 5s | Blocking: No (silent when healthy)

What it does
Catches the failure a hook cannot report about itself: never running at all. At session start it checks three things and stays silent unless one fails:

Every hook command in .claude/settings.json and settings.local.json points at a file that exists (and, for shell scripts, is executable).
Errors logged in .claude/state/hook-log.jsonl since the last check.
Liveness: a hook on PreToolUse or PostToolUse that has logged nothing across three or more logged sessions is configured but not running.



Exit behavior
Always exits 0. Problems go to you as a systemMessage and to Claude as additionalContext, with an instruction to mention them before other work.

title: Hooks & Automation
text:
8. Git hooks: pre-commit and post-merge
These are git hooks, not Claude Code hooks. They live in .githooks/; scripts/install-hooks.sh points git at that folder (git config core.hooksPath .githooks) once per clone.
pre-commit runs on every commit, including ones made outside Claude:

blocks when scripts/check_scaffold.py finds a broken reference, a missing hook file, or a weight that disagrees between permissions.md and quality-gates.json
blocks when .claude/hooks/ or settings changed and scripts/test_hooks.py fails, or when enforcement scripts changed and scripts/test_scripts.py fails
blocks on HIGH lint findings in staged analysis scripts (setwd(), absolute paths, …)
prints paper-coherence findings for staged .tex files as advice; they block at /submit

Bypass with SKIP_GATE=1 git commit ... and say why in the message. It does not check the quality score; /tools commit does that once critics have scored.
post-merge
Event: Git post-merge | Blocking: No
A standard Git hook (not a Claude Code hook) that prints a reminder after any git merge or git pull to update the session report.
#!/bin/bash
echo "=== SESSION MERGED TO MAIN ==="
echo ""
echo "Remember to append a summary to SESSION_REPORT.md if you haven't already."
Merges to main are significant project events that should be logged. This hook is a simple reminder — it does not enforce logging, just nudges.

title: Hooks & Automation
text:
Step 1: Write the script
Create a new file in .claude/hooks/. Make it executable.
touch .claude/hooks/my-custom-hook.sh
chmod +x .claude/hooks/my-custom-hook.sh

title: Hooks & Automation
text:
Step 2: Write the logic
The script receives the tool input as JSON on stdin (for PreToolUse and PostToolUse); the edited file path is tool_input.file_path. To show Claude a message from a PostToolUse hook, print JSON with hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext.
Here is an example hook that warns when a LaTeX file is edited without compiling:
#!/bin/bash
# warn-latex-compile.sh --- Advisory reminder after LaTeX edits

FILE=$(python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin).get("tool_input",{}).get("file_path",""))')
[[ -z "$FILE" ]] && exit 0

# Only fire on .tex files
case "$FILE" in
  *.tex) ;;
  *) exit 0 ;;
esac

MSG="LaTeX file edited: $FILE. Compile with: cd paper && latexmk main.tex"
python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.dumps({"hookSpecificOutput":{"hookEventName":"PostToolUse","additionalContext":sys.argv[1]}}))' "$MSG"

exit 0

title: Hooks & Automation
Hooks & Automation
text:
Step 4: Test
The simplest test is to trigger the event. For a PostToolUse hook on Edit|Write, just ask Claude to edit a file matching your hook’s filter. Watch for the hook’s output in the transcript.
For standalone testing of the script itself (and add a case to scripts/test_hooks.py so it stays tested):
echo '{"tool_name": "Edit", "tool_input": {"file_path": "paper/main.tex"}}' \
  | CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR="$(pwd)" .claude/hooks/my-custom-hook.sh
echo "Exit code: $?"

title: Hooks & Automation
text:
Example: Lint before Claude commits






Note



You don’t need this for clo-author itself: the git pre-commit gate in .githooks/pre-commit (see Git hooks) already blocks HIGH lint findings on every commit, including commits made outside Claude. The example shows how a Claude-side PreToolUse hook on Bash works.


A hook that runs the linter before every git commit command Claude issues:
#!/bin/bash
# pre-commit-lint.sh --- Lint all staged R/Python/Julia files before commit

INPUT=$(cat)
TOOL=$(echo "$INPUT" | jq -r '.tool_name')
COMMAND=$(echo "$INPUT" | jq -r '.tool_input.command // empty')

# Only fire on Bash tool calls that are git commits
[[ "$TOOL" != "Bash" ]] && exit 0
[[ "$COMMAND" != git\ commit* ]] && exit 0

# Find staged script files
STAGED=$(git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=ACM \
  | grep -E '\.(R|py|jl)$' || true)

if [[ -n "$STAGED" ]]; then
  echo "Linting staged scripts before commit..."
  for f in $STAGED; do
    "$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR"/.claude/hooks/lint-scripts.sh "$f"
  done
fi

exit 0  # Advisory only --- change to exit 2 to block on lint failures
Register it under PreToolUse with matcher "Bash":
{
  "matcher": "Bash",
  "hooks": [
    {
      "type": "command",
      "command": "\"$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR\"/.claude/hooks/pre-commit-lint.sh",
      "timeout": 15
    }
  ]
}
